The Piedmont region of the southeastern United States has experienced widespread forest regrowth over the past century due to agricultural abandonment. Today’s landscapes are largely characterized by mature forests that are becoming increasingly fragmented by suburbanization. Here, we assessed the filtering effects of forest age, landscape forest cover (LFC), and deadwood volume on saproxylic beetles in northeastern Georgia. Using historic aerial imagery to distinguish forest age (young = regrown after 1938; old = mature in 1938), we sampled beetles in mature forests of both age classes occurring along an LFC gradient. We measured five traits with hypothesized functional roles (body length, body width, body roundness, antenna length, eye length) for the 472 species captured. Using a joint species distribution model (JSDM), we tested trait-niche relationships (i.e., how traits influence species’ responses) and estimated community trait composition (mean and dispersion of trait values) along gradients of environmental filters.

Table 2 Hypothesized trait-niche and community trait composition relationships for five beetle morphological traits and three environmental filters (covariates) used in the joint species distribution model (JSDM). Justifications for each hypothesis are included. Observed relationships supported with > 85 % posterior probability from the JSDM are shown, and sign (positive: +, negative: -) is indicated. Relative support values are +++/— (>95 %), ++/– (>90 %), +/- (>85 %). Detailed summaries of the functional roles of traits are found in Table 1. LFC = Landscape Forest Cover.

The dominant vegetation in the Piedmont region is oak (Quercus)- pine (Pinus) forest (Spooner et al., 2021). During stand development, forest composition transitions from pine dominance in early years to eventual hardwood (and especially oak) dominance after a century or more (Oosting, 1942; Nicholson and Monk, 1974; Orwig and Abrams, 1994). Other species, such as tuliptree (Liriodendron tulipifera), sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua), and red maple (Acer rurbum) can also occur in great numbers locally, especially on mesic sites. Oak-pine ecosystems were historically maintained with occasional, low severity fire (Spooner et al., 2021). However, due to fire suppression, forests developing today may be undergoing alternative successional trajectories favoring more mesic species (Nowacki and Abrams, 2008).
![Image block](doc:44f6c52/tier:advanced/page:4/block:3)

To determine landscape forest cover, we digitized forest cover in the current landscape by manually creating polygons in ArcMap 10.4 (Esri, Redlands, California) over 1-m satellite imagery from 2017 (U.S. Geological Survey, 2017; Traylor et al., 2023a; Fig. 1A). The proportion of the landscape covered in forest within a 2000 m radius was then measured, hereafter referred to as landscape forest cover (LFC). This radius was chosen because it had the highest correlation with saproxylic beetle species richness out of eight radii (250–2,000 m; Traylor et al., 2023a), indicating it is the appropriate spatial scale based on the recommended procedures in Holland et al. (2004) and Jackson and Fahrig (2015). Both young mature and old mature forests were distributed along this LFC gradient such that mean LFC did not differ between age groups at any spatial scale investigated (Traylor et al., 2023a). The minimum distance between any two sites was >1,000 m.

To assess how traits influence species’ responses to three filters (forest age, LFC, and deadwood volume), we created a joint species distribution model (JSDM) in the hierarchical modelling of species communities (HMSC) package (Tikhonov et al., 2020) in R (R Core Team, 2022). Briefly, this procedure fits a multivariate, hierarchical generalized linear mixed model to a matrix of species occurrence or abundance data using Bayesian inference. The model estimates a niche for each species (β parameters) with respect to each environmental co-variate, and the role of traits in defining species’ niches is also estimated (γ), as is the residual phylogenetic correlation in niches unexplained by traits (ρ). Species’ niches are thus jointly (i.e., non-independently) estimated due to a hierarchical layer in the model which incorporates trait effects and improves estimation for less frequently collected species (Ovaskainen and Abrego, 2020).

After omitting species present at fewer than five sites, which are too rare to model effectively (Ovaskainen and Abrego, 2020), we fit a presence/absence JSDM on a matrix of 194 species at 40 sites using a probit link function to a Bernoulli distribution. We included five traits (described above) that have well-defined functional relevance and for which we could produce testable hypotheses in relation to covariates (Brousseau et al., 2018). Our model had six fixed-effect covariates: three focal covariates for which we produced hypotheses (forest age (categorical: old, young), LFC, and deadwood volume; Table 2) and three additional covariates that were included to improve predictive power (gap fraction, tree diversity, and Tree Axis 2). These additional covariates are known to be important for saproxylic beetle communities (Lettenmaier et al., 2022; Traylor et al., 2022a), and thus may be relevant to species occurrences as well. Deadwood volume and gap fraction were transformed using $\log ( \mathbf { x } + 1 )$ and log(x) to improve linearity, respectively. These traits and covariates had acceptable variance inflation factors less than three, checked using the faraway R package (Faraway, 2016). HMSC scales all covariates and traits to zero mean and unit variance for model fitting. Additionally, because morphological traits are correlated across the Coleoptera phylogeny (Hagge et al., 2021), we included a phylogenetic correlation matrix in the covariance structure of the model. This was done by first creating a tree based on hierarchical taxonomic relationships (using the levels suborder, series, superfamily, family, subfamily, genus, and species) with all branch lengths equal to 1 using the ape package (Paradis and Schliep, 2019). This method underestimates deep divergence $( \mathbf { e . g . } ,$ between families or superfamilies and higher) and overestimates recent divergence (e.g., between species within a genus), but is still recommended when no phylogeny is available (Ovaskainen and Abrego, 2020). Taxonomic levels followed Beutel and Leschen (2005) and Leschen et al. (2010), except for the newly supported superfamilies in Cai et al. (2022). All tips (species) were kept at equal lengths from the root despite taxonomic levels missing for some groups (e.g., there are no classified subfamilies in Aderidae but a dummy subfamily level was included for consistency, Supplementary Table S4). To account for the spatial layout of our study

We sampled the posterior distribution of the JSDM using default priors with four Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains, each run for 35,000 iterations with the first $^ { 1 0 , 0 0 0 }$ discarded as burn in. Remaining iterations were thinned by 100 to produce 250 samples per MCMC chain (1,000 total samples). Convergence and sample independence were checked with potential scale reduction factors (Gelman and Rubin, 1992) and effective sample sizes (ESS), respectively. Explanatory power was estimated by averaging across species for the area under the curve (AUC) and Tjur $\mathtt { R } ^ { 2 }$ . To assess predictive power, we performed 10-fold cross-validation, where sampling sites were randomly assigned into 10 folds, and each fold was used for validation based on predictions from the other nine folds. Mean values of AUC and $\operatorname { T j u r } \operatorname { R } ^ { 2 }$ were obtained from the cross-validation procedure. We additionally used variance partitioning to estimate the amount of variance that was explained by each covariate and the amount of variance explained by traits for species responses and occurrences.

Figure S1). Although poor on average, predictive Tjur $\mathrm { R } ^ { 2 }$ was positive for 98 species and predictive AUC was > 0.5 for 104 species (53–56 % of species, not including nine species that were present in all sites), and these values were not correlated to species’ prevalence (Supplementary Figure S1). Variance partitioning showed that traits altogether explained 13.7 % of the total explained variance in species occurrences. Additionally, 4.6–16.4 % of the explained variance in species niches (β) can be explained by the traits, with forest age having the highest value followed by gap fraction at 12.4 % (Supplementary Table S5). There was very little residual phylogenetic signal in the model (mean ρ-parameter = 0.154, 95 % CI = 0–0.530), and the random spatial effect showed some evidence of spatial autocorrelation at approximately 1,163 m (mean α-parameter, 95 % CI = 0–9,728 m). Overall, many more species responded positively than negatively to forest age $\mathbf { ( i . e . , }$ β-parameter showed higher probability of occurring in old mature forest), LFC, and deadwood volume at > 95 % and > 85 % posterior probability (pp, Table 3). Species responding with > 95 % pp to any covariate(s) can be found in Table 4. All species responses with > 85 % pp, and 95 % credible intervals of β for all species, can be found in Supplementary Tables S6 & S7, respectively.

Positive (+) and negative (-) responses indicate higher/lower occurrence probability in old mature forests, with higher landscape forest cover (LFC), with higher deadwood volume, in more mesic tree communities, with higher gap fraction, and with higher tree diversity, respectively. Fig. 3. Community trait composition (mean and dispersion) of five morphological traits of saproxylic beetles along gradients of three environmental filters (covariates). Effects were estimated from a joint species distribution model. Mean estimates are shown with 95 % credible intervals. Relationships supported with >85 % posterior probability (pp) are shown in blue (negative) and red (positive). Grey dots represent values from sampled communities. Trait values of body width, antenna length, and eye length are standardized according to body length, and body length is log transformed (refer to Methods section 2.2). LFC = landscape forest cover; DW = deadwood.

Figure S1. Comparison of predictive power (predicted Tjur R 2 and area under the curve (AUC) from 10-fold cross validation) to saproxylic beetle species prevalence (top row) and explanatory power (bottom row). Dots represent species used in the joint species distribution model (excluding nine species which were present at all sites, and thus were not included in predictive power estimates). Top row: predictive power was not related to species prevalence (i.e., the proportion of sites they occurred at), indicating that predictive power was not stronger for more common species. Mean predictive power (red vertical line) was positive but close to 0 for Tjur R 2 and 0.5 for AUC. Bottom row: Predictive power was always lower than, but strongly correlated to, explanatory power. Diagonal line represents a perfect relationship, horizontal line shows cut off for positive predictive power (0 for Tjur R 2 , 0.5 for AUC).
![Image block](doc:d15ce8c/tier:flash/page:2/block:1)

Figure S2. Trait-niche relationships (γ-parameter) between standardized trait values for saproxylic beetles (x-axis) and standardized environmental covariates (y-axis) from the joint species distribution model. Each dot represents a species’ estimated mean niche (β-parameter) for a covariate plotted against its standardized trait value. Species are colored according to having a positive (red) or negative (blue) niche at higher than 85% posterior probability. Black regression lines show post-hoc best-fit relationships between species traits and β estimates; for γ parameter estimates quantifying these relationships, and their posterior support, refer to Fig. 1 in the main text and Table S9.

Figure S3. Relationships between community trait mean and dispersion of five morphological traits across all saproxylic beetle species sampled (x axis; n = 472) and the 194 species used in the joint species distribution model (y axis). Each dot represents the beetle community at a single site. Species collected at fewer than five sites (n = 278) were excluded from the model because they were too rare to accurately model. Pearson correlations range from 0.837–0.949 (community trait mean) and 0.807–0.898 (community trait dispersion)

Trait | Indicated functional role
Body length | Larger beetles have longer development times, lower fecundity/ abundance, require larger pieces of deadwood, and may be poorer dispersers (Foit, 2010; Brin et al., 2011; Fountain-Jones et al., 2015; Brin et al., 2016; Gillespie et al., 2017).
Body width | Wider beetles are thought to rely on resources found outside of the phloem layer, such as decayed wood or tree cavities. Thus, wider species may be poorer dispersers based on habitat stability and have longer development times compared to narrower species (Micó et al., 2020; Hagge et al., 2021).
Roundness | Rounder beetles are thought to rely on resources found outside of the phloem layer, such as decayed wood or tree cavities. Thus, rounder species may be poorer dispersers based on habitat stability and have longer development times compared to flatter species (Micó et al., 2020; Hagge et al., 2021).
Antennae length | Longer antennae allow for better resource detection and olfactory communication, and thus longer antenna may be related to better dispersal ability or increased flight activity (Elgar et al., 2018; Javoïs et al., 2019; Neff et al., 2022).
Eye length | Larger eyes allow for better resource detection (Talarico et al., 2007, 2011), but may also be related to preferring more open habitats (e.g., tree hollows) as compared to confined habitats (e.g., under bark; Micó et al., 2020).
